evidence.claim: Follow the Logan River through limestone cliffs toward Bear Lake.
evidence.quote: The byway runs alongside the winding Logan River from the city of Logan to Garden City. Much of the corridor travels through spectacular, craggy limestone cliffs. The scenic byway peaks at a glorious vista overlooking the turquoise waters of Bear Lake

evidence.claim: US 89 follows the Logan River between limestone cliffs, climbing through Logan Canyon before descending steeply toward Bear Lake Valley.
evidence.quote: The byway runs alongside the winding Logan River from the city of Logan to Garden City. Much of the corridor travels through spectacular, craggy limestone cliffs.

evidence.claim: US 89 follows the Logan River between limestone cliffs, climbing through Logan Canyon before descending steeply toward Bear Lake Valley.
evidence.quote: Just beyond the summit is a steep road leading into Bear Lake Valley

evidence.claim: The Forest Service describes this National Scenic Byway as a winding journey northeast through national forest, with fossil-bearing canyon walls exposing 500 million years of geologic history.
evidence.quote: From historic Cache Valley on the west, this byway winds northeast through the national forest to Bear Lake spanning the Utah/Idaho border. Along the way, 500 million years of geologic history unfold in the lower canyon's deeply incised walls and formations laden with fossils.

evidence.claim: Thomas E. Ricks had settled in Cache Valley in 1859, when Logan Canyon supplied timber and other resources to nearby settlements.
evidence.quote: Thomas E. Ricks settled in the nearby Cache Valley in 1859. Logan Canyon was an area rich with timber and other resources for nearby settlements

evidence.claim: The road began as a connection to Bear Lake Valley: at Brigham Young’s recommendation, Ricks and other community members undertook its construction.
evidence.quote: At the recommendation of Brigham Young, Ricks and others in the community began constructing a road to Bear Lake Valley.

evidence.claim: The section reaching Ricks Spring was completed first, before winter; that road is now part of US 89 and the scenic byway.
evidence.quote: The road to Ricks Spring was the first section to be completed before winter

evidence.claim: that road is now part of US 89 and the scenic byway.
evidence.quote: The road is now part of the Logan Canyon Scenic Byway, part of US Route 89.

evidence.claim: National designation in 2002 also changed the corridor: the stretch north from Garden City to the Idaho line became part of the Bear Lake Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: Shortened June 13, 2002 when designated a National Scenic Byway and the portion of US-89 from Garden City to the Utah and Idaho State Line was transferred to the Bear Lake Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: Beginning at 1500 East in Logan, the route connects Cache Valley with Bear Lake Valley.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 89 through the canyon has been designated a National Scenic Byway and connects the Cache and Bear Lake valleys.

evidence.claim: Beginning at 1500 East in Logan,
evidence.quote: US Route 89, beginning at 1500 East in Logan

evidence.claim: The canyon climbs about 2,900 feet to approximately 7,800 feet above sea level.
evidence.quote: The canyon rises to an elevation of approximately 7,800 feet (2,400 m) above sea level, after a vertical climb of about 2,900 feet (880 m).

evidence.claim: Beyond the summit, overlooks face Bear Lake and the road drops steeply into its valley.
evidence.quote: Just beyond the summit is a steep road leading into Bear Lake Valley and scenic overlooks that provide views of deep blue Bear Lake.

evidence.claim: The designated corridor finishes at SR 30 in Garden City.
evidence.quote: US Route 89, beginning at 1500 East in Logan and running to the intersection of SR-30 in Garden City

evidence.claim: Often credited with more than 3,000 years, this Rocky Mountain juniper yielded core samples in the 1950s that put its age at around 1,500 years.
evidence.quote: The Jardine Juniper is an individual of the species Rocky Mountain juniper found within Logan Canyon in the Cache National Forest. Often credited with an age of over 3,000 years, core samples taken in the 1950s revealed that it was around 1,500 years old.

evidence.claim: It stands approximately 40 feet tall in Logan Canyon.
evidence.quote: It stands approximately 40 feet (12 m) tall

evidence.claim: Maurice Blood Linford found it in 1923 while a student at Utah State Agricultural College.
evidence.quote: Discovered in 1923 by Maurice Blood Linford while he was a student at Utah State Agricultural College (USAC)

evidence.claim: Its name honors another alumnus, William Marion Jardine, who served as U.S. secretary of agriculture.
evidence.quote: it was named after USAC alumnus and former U.S. Secretary of Agriculture William Marion Jardine

evidence.claim: Ricks Spring brings river water back out of the rock.
evidence.quote: The spring is not an artesian source, but comes from the Logan River.

evidence.claim: Visitors once took jugs and barrels home, mistaking the water for the product of a deep aquifer; giardia made many of them sick.
evidence.quote: people visiting the spring often drank from it, bringing home jugs and barrels of the "fresh spring water" under the assumption it came from a deep aquifer. They often became sick with giardia

evidence.claim: Hydrogeologists suspected the link in the 1950s after noticing a pattern in the flows.
evidence.quote: In the 1950s hydrogeologists noticed a pattern between the flows of the Logan River and theorized a connection between them.

evidence.claim: In 1972, dye placed in the Logan River appeared at the spring, confirming the connection.
evidence.quote: Later that summer dye tracing was used in the Logan River and the dye was found in Ricks Spring, confirming the water source of the spring.
In 1972, a severe winter froze the river

evidence.claim: Further tracing linked it to minor streams and Tony Grove Lake as well.
evidence.quote: Several minor streams, located as far as five miles away, and up to 2600 feet higher in elevation, also feed into the underground network that feeds Ricks Spring. Water from Tony Grove Lake also contributes to Ricks Spring.

evidence.claim: Water eroded passages through fractured limestone, making a route from higher inflows to this cave outflow.
evidence.quote: Over time water flowing through these points eroded through the limestone creating a path from the river and other inflows at high elevation to flow and emit from the spring.

evidence.claim: fractured limestone
evidence.quote: Pressure and earthquakes have caused the rock to fold and fracture exposing weak points.

evidence.claim: this cave outflow
evidence.quote: a natural water outflow from a cave in Logan Canyon

evidence.claim: The overlooks beyond Logan Canyon’s summit reveal Bear Lake before the descent into its valley.
evidence.quote: Just beyond the summit is a steep road leading into Bear Lake Valley and scenic overlooks that provide views of deep blue Bear Lake.

evidence.claim: Its turquoise-blue color comes from suspended calcium carbonate deposits that refract light.
evidence.quote: its unique turquoise-blue color, which is due to the refraction of calcium carbonate (limestone) deposits suspended in the lake.

evidence.claim: This natural lake straddles Utah and Idaho, occupying a basin formed by fault subsidence that continues to deepen its eastern side.
evidence.quote: Bear Lake is a natural freshwater lake on the Idaho–Utah border in the Western United States.

evidence.claim: occupying a basin formed by fault subsidence that continues to deepen its eastern side.
evidence.quote: It was formed by fault subsidence that continues today, slowly deepening the lake along the eastern side.

evidence.claim: Its relationship with the Bear River changed in 1911, when a diversion directed most of the river’s flow into the lake through Mud Lake.
evidence.quote: In 1911 a diversion was constructed at Wardboro, Idaho that redirected the majority of the flow of the Bear River into Bear Lake via Mud Lake.

evidence.claim: An outlet canal returns the water to the Bear River.
evidence.quote: Water then exits Bear Lake via an outlet canal to rejoin the Bear River.

evidence.claim: That connection allows water to be stored for irrigation later in the year.
evidence.quote: storing spring runoff for irrigation later in the year.

evidence.claim: Notice the lake’s turquoise-blue water, colored by suspended calcium carbonate.
evidence.quote: its unique turquoise-blue color, which is due to the refraction of calcium carbonate (limestone) deposits suspended in the lake.
